primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration is nonfunctioning dysplastic lung tissue without a normal tracheobronchial connection that lies within the visceral pleura of adjacent lung. It receives anomalous systemic arterial blood, most often from the descending thoracic aorta, and usually drains through the pulmonary veins.
vignette: A 22-year-old woman has had three episodes of pneumonia involving the same posterior basal region of the left lower lobe. CT shows an abnormal segment of lung that lies within the same visceral pleural covering as the adjacent normal lung and has no normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree. Intralobar pulmonary sequestration is suspected.
lead: Which combination of arterial supply and venous drainage is most likely in this lesion?
correct: Arterial supply from the descending thoracic aorta with venous drainage to the pulmonary veins
distractors: Arterial supply from the pulmonary artery with venous drainage to the pulmonary veins
Arterial supply from the descending thoracic aorta with venous drainage to the azygos or hemiazygos system
Arterial supply from the pulmonary artery with venous drainage to the azygos or hemiazygos system
Arterial supply from bronchial arteries with venous drainage directly to the superior vena cava
distractor_notes: Pulmonary arterial inflow with pulmonary venous drainage is the usual pulmonary circulation of functioning lung; a sequestration is defined by anomalous systemic arterial supply.

Systemic arterial supply with systemic venous drainage is characteristic of extralobar sequestration more than intralobar sequestration. Extralobar lesions have their own pleural covering, whereas this lesion shares visceral pleura with adjacent lung.
Pulmonary arterial inflow is not the defining vascular supply of pulmonary sequestration, and systemic venous drainage would not match the usual intralobar pattern.

Although bronchial arteries are systemic vessels, the typical anomalous arterial supply of pulmonary sequestration arises from the descending thoracic aorta or another systemic artery, and intralobar lesions usually drain to pulmonary veins rather than directly to the superior vena cava.
key_expl: The lesion is intralobar pulmonary sequestration because it is nonfunctioning lung without normal tracheobronchial communication and lies within the visceral pleura of the adjacent lung. Pulmonary sequestrations receive anomalous systemic arterial supply, most commonly from the descending thoracic aorta. Intralobar sequestrations usually drain through the pulmonary veins; in contrast, extralobar sequestrations have a separate pleural covering and more often drain through systemic veins such as the azygos or hemiazygos system.
objective: Distinguish intralobar from extralobar pulmonary sequestration by pleural relationship and vascular anatomy: intralobar lesions typically have systemic arterial supply and pulmonary venous drainage.
clues: recurrent infection in the same lower-lobe region
lesion lies within the same visceral pleura as adjacent lung

sources.support: NCBI defines pulmonary sequestration as dysplastic nonfunctioning lung without normal tracheobronchial communication and with anomalous systemic vascular supply. It states that intralobar sequestration lies within the visceral pleura of functioning lung, usually drains to a pulmonary vein, and commonly receives systemic arterial supply from the descending thoracic aorta; extralobar sequestration has a separate pleura and systemic venous drainage.
